  • The main ones → count, for_each, depends_on, provider, lifecycle
  • Terraform has no real loops → count and for_each are how you get loop-like behaviour → it builds every copy in one plan, not step by step

docs.title: count
docs.text:
• count = N → creates N copies of the block, identified by number → aws_s3_bucket.bucket1[0], [1], [2]
  • count.index → zero-based number of the current copy → runs 0 to count - 1 → only valid inside a block that sets count
  • Without count.index every copy gets the same config → two buckets with the same name fail
  • count = length(var.list) → follows the list size automatically → never goes out of range
  • On/off toggle → count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0
  • Weakness → copies are tied to position → remove an item from the middle and the later ones shift down → Terraform destroys and recreates them
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket1" {
  count  = length(var.bucket_names)
  bucket = var.bucket_names[count.index]

  tags = var.tag-s3
}

variable "bucket_names" {
  description = "list of bucket names"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["my-unique-ap14-tf", "my-unique-ap1404-tf", "my-unique-ap140604-tf"]
}

docs.title: for_each
docs.text:
• for_each → creates one copy per item, identified by name → aws_s3_bucket.bucket2["my-unique-ap14-tf"]
  • Accepts only a map or a set of strings → not a number, not a plain list → convert a list with toset(var.list)
  • each.key / each.value → the for_each version of count.index
  • Set → each.key and each.value are the same thing, the item itself → use each.value
  • Map → each.key is the left side, each.value is the right side
  • Sets have no index → var.set[each.key] does not work
  • Cannot use count and for_each on the same block
  • Remove one item → only that copy is destroyed → the rest are untouched
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket2" {
  for_each = toset(var.bucket_names)
  bucket   = each.value

  tags = var.tag-s3
}

docs.title: With a map
docs.text:
variable "bucket_map" {
  description = "map of purpose => bucket name"
  type        = map(string)
  default = {
    logs   = "my-unique-ap14-logs-tf"
    data   = "my-unique-ap1404-data-tf"
    backup = "my-unique-ap140604-backup-tf"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket3" {
  for_each = var.bucket_map
  bucket   = each.value

  tags = merge(var.tag-s3, {
    Purpose = each.key
  })
}

output "bucket_arns" {
  value = { for k, b in aws_s3_bucket.bucket3 : k => b.arn }
}
  • each.value → the real bucket name
  • each.key → label used for the Purpose tag
  • merge() → combines the existing tag map with the extra tag (assumes tag-s3 is a map(string))
  • for expression in output → builds a map of purpose => arn

docs.title: count vs for_each
docs.text: count for_each Identified by number [0] name ["logs"] Input a number map or set of strings Current item count.index each.key / each.value Remove from the middle later copies shift, may be recreated only that copy is destroyed Best for N identical copies, on/off toggle distinct things that each have an identity

docs.title: depends_on
docs.text:
• depends_on → forces one resource to be created after another when Terraform cannot see the link
  • Normal ordering → Terraform reads references → if B uses an attribute of A, A goes first (implicit dependency)
  • Needed only for hidden dependencies → B needs A but never references it → e.g. an IAM policy that must exist before an instance boots
  • Takes a list of resource references, no attributes → [aws_iam_role_policy.s3_access], not [aws_iam_role_policy.s3_access.id]
  • Works on modules too → depends_on = [module.network]
  • Destroy order is reversed
  • Use sparingly → prefer a real reference → overuse makes plans less precise
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  ami                  = "ami-123"
  instance_type        = "t3.micro"
  iam_instance_profile = aws_iam_instance_profile.app.name

  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.s3_access]
}

docs.title: provider and lifecycle
docs.text:
• provider → picks a non-default provider config, e.g. an alias for another region → provider = aws.mumbai
  • Modules use providers = { aws = aws.mumbai } (plural)
  • lifecycle → controls create, update and destroy behaviour
lifecycle {
  create_before_destroy = true
  prevent_destroy       = true
  ignore_changes        = [tags]
  replace_triggered_by  = [aws_launch_template.lt]
}
  • create_before_destroy → build the new one first, then delete the old
  • prevent_destroy → any plan that would destroy it errors out → safety rail for prod databases
  • ignore_changes → ignore drift on the listed attributes
  • replace_triggered_by → replace this resource when the listed one changes

docs.title: Lab: count and for_each on S3 buckets
docs.text:
Errors I hit while practising:

Symptom Cause Fix Invalid index on var.bucket_names[count.index] count = 4 but the list has 3 items, so index 3 does not exist Use count = length(var.bucket_names) The given "for_each" argument value is unsuitable for_each = length(...) passes a number Pass a set or map: for_each = toset(var.bucket_names) Cannot look up var.bucket_set_names[each.key] A set has no index Use each.value directly

Notes:

  • count = 2 with a 3-item list → creates only the first two buckets, the third name is ignored
  • The plan fails before anything is created → no partial apply

Interview points

  • What is a meta-argument? → an argument available on any resource regardless of provider, e.g. count, for_each, depends_on, provider, lifecycle
  • What is count.index? → the zero-based index of the current copy of a resource that uses count
  • count vs for_each? → count identifies copies by position, for_each by key → prefer for_each for distinct resources
  • Why is for_each safer than count when removing an item? → with count the indexes shift and later resources get destroyed and recreated, with for_each only the removed key is touched
  • What types does for_each accept? → a map or a set of strings, so wrap a list in toset()
  • What are each.key and each.value for a set? → both are the item itself
  • What happens with count = 4 on a 3-item list? → plan fails with Invalid index, nothing is created
  • Can you use count and for_each on the same resource? → no
  • When do you need depends_on? → only for hidden dependencies, where B needs A but does not reference any of its attributes
  • What does prevent_destroy do? → makes Terraform error on any plan that would destroy the resource

docs.title: Providers & Versioning
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Terraform course day 2

docs.title: What is a provider
docs.text:
• Provider → a plugin that lets Terraform talk to an external API (AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, GitHub, Cloudflare, Datadog)
  • Terraform core only knows HCL, state and the dependency graph → it has no idea how to create an EC2 instance; the AWS provider turns your resource blocks into AWS API calls
  • Each provider defines its own resource types and data sources → aws_instance, aws_vpc, github_repository
  • Separate binary → downloaded by terraform init, not bundled with Terraform
  • Not only clouds → random, local, tls, http, null are utility providers

docs.title: Where providers come from
docs.text:
• Terraform Registry → registry.terraform.io, the default source
  • Official → maintained by HashiCorp (hashicorp/aws, hashicorp/random)
  • Partner → maintained by the vendor, verified by HashiCorp (cloudflare/cloudflare, datadog/datadog)
  • Community → maintained by individuals, check activity and stars before trusting one
  • Source address → [hostname/]namespace/type, e.g. hashicorp/aws = registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws

docs.title: Reading the provider docs
docs.text:
• Registry → AWS provider → Documentation → search a resource like aws_vpc
  • Example Usage → copy-paste starting point
  • Argument Reference → what you can set; each argument is marked required or optional
  • Attribute Reference → what the resource exposes after creation (id, arn), used in references
  • Import → how to bring an existing resource under Terraform

docs.title: Core version vs provider version
docs.text:
• Terraform core → the terraform binary (e.g. 1.9.x), parses config, manages state, builds the plan
  • Provider → one plugin per platform (e.g. AWS 6.x), its own release cycle, much more frequent than core
  • Pin core → required_version | pin providers → required_providers
  • terraform version → shows core and every installed provider

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}
  • terraform {} → settings for Terraform itself, not for any cloud
  • required_providers → which plugins this project needs
  • aws = → local name, used in provider "aws" and matched to resource prefixes (aws_)
  • source → where to download it from
  • version → which versions are acceptable
  • provider "aws" {} → how to configure it: region, default tags, assume role
  • terraform {} decides what to download (used by init) | provider {} is used at plan / apply

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• Never in the .tf file → it's committed to Git
  • The AWS provider looks for credentials in this order (simplified):
    1. Env vars → AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_PROFILE
    2. Shared files → ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.aws/config (from aws configure)
    3. IAM role → EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, or OIDC in CI
  • Best practice → short-lived credentials: SSO locally, OIDC role in GitHub Actions, no long-lived access keys

docs.title: Why pin versions
docs.text:
• Compatibility → a provider version needs a minimum core version
  • Stability → major versions (5.x → 6.x) contain breaking changes: renamed arguments, removed resources
  • Reproducibility → same versions on my laptop, a teammate's laptop and CI
  • Features → new AWS services only appear in newer provider versions
  • Fixes → bug and security fixes come in minor and patch releases
  • Unpinned → init on a new machine silently pulls the latest major, and a plan that worked yesterday breaks today

docs.title: Version constraints
docs.text:
• = 1.2.3 (or just 1.2.3) → exactly this version
  • != 1.2.3 → anything except this one (to skip a known-bad release)
  • >= 1.2 / > 1.2 / <= 1.2 / < 1.2 → bounds
  • >= 1.2, < 2.0 → range, commas mean AND
  • ~> → pessimistic constraint: only the rightmost number you wrote can go up, everything left of it is locked
Constraint Means Allows Blocks ~> 6.1.1 >= 6.1.1, < 6.2.0 6.1.2, 6.1.9 6.2.0, 7.0 ~> 6.1 >= 6.1, < 7.0 6.2, 6.50 7.0 ~> 6.0 >= 6.0, < 7.0 any 6.x 7.0
  • ~> never goes below what you wrote → ~> 6.1.1 won't pick 6.1.0
  • Common choice → ~> 6.0 for providers (all of 6.x, no surprise major upgrade)

docs.title: Lock file
docs.text:
• terraform init → picks the newest version matching the constraint, downloads it into .terraform/, writes the exact version and checksums to .terraform.lock.hcl
  • Next init → uses the locked version, even if a newer one matching the constraint exists
  • terraform init -upgrade → ignore the lock, take the newest allowed version, rewrite the lock
  • Commit .terraform.lock.hcl → everyone and CI get the same provider build | don't commit .terraform/ (binaries, hundreds of MB)
  • terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 → record checksums for other OSes, so a Mac teammate and a Linux CI runner both pass verification
  • Constraint vs lock → constraint is the allowed range, lock is the exact version chosen inside it

docs.title: Multiple providers and aliases
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
    random = {
      source  = "hashicorp/random"
      version = "~> 3.6"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"            # default
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "mumbai"
  region = "ap-south-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "backup" {
  provider = aws.mumbai
  bucket   = "my-backup-bucket"
}
  • A provider block without alias → the default for every aws_ resource
  • alias → a second configuration of the same provider, picked with provider = aws.<alias>
  • Use cases → multi-region (DR copies), multi-account (assume role into another account)

docs.title: Lab: first script
docs.text:
# providers.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

# main.tf
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"

  tags = {
    Name = "tf-lab-vpc"
  }
}

resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24"

  tags = {
    Name = "tf-lab-public"
  }
}
  1. terraform init → downloads the AWS provider, creates .terraform/ and .terraform.lock.hcl
  2. terraform fmt and terraform validate
  3. terraform plan → Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
  4. terraform apply → VPC first, then the subnet, because the subnet references aws_vpc.main.id

  5. terraform destroy → removes both, subnet first

  6. vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id → internal reference: the VPC ID isn't known until AWS creates it, so it shows as (known after apply) in the plan

  7. Optional arguments not set → provider defaults apply (e.g. instance_tenancy = "default")
Symptom Cause Fix Inconsistent dependency lock file Constraint changed after the lock was written terraform init -upgrade No valid credential sources found No AWS credentials found aws configure or export AWS_PROFILE Unsupported Terraform Core version Local terraform older than required_version Upgrade Terraform Could not load plugin / provider not found Skipped init or typo in source Fix source, rerun terraform init

Quick revision

  • Provider = plugin that turns HCL into API calls, downloaded by init
  • required_providers → what to download, provider {} → how to configure it
  • ~> → only the rightmost written number can increase
  • Commit .terraform.lock.hcl, never .terraform/

Interview points

  • What is a Terraform provider? → a plugin that implements resources and data sources for an API and translates HCL into API calls
  • Why pin provider versions? → major versions have breaking changes; pinning keeps plans reproducible across machines and CI
  • What does ~> 6.1 allow? → >= 6.1, < 7.0, any 6.x from 6.1 up
  • What does ~> 6.1.1 allow? → >= 6.1.1, < 6.2.0, patch releases only
  • What is .terraform.lock.hcl? → records the exact provider versions and checksums chosen by init; commit it so everyone uses the same build
  • Constraint vs lock file? → constraint is the allowed range, the lock is the exact version picked inside it; init -upgrade moves it
  • How do you deploy to two regions in one config? → a second provider block with alias, then provider = aws.<alias> on the resources
  • Where should AWS credentials come from? → env vars, an AWS profile or an IAM role / OIDC; never hardcoded in .tf files
  • Terraform core vs provider version? → core is the CLI binary pinned by required_version; providers are separate plugins pinned in required_providers, each with its own releases

docs.title: State & Remote Backend
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Terraform course day 4

docs.title: How Terraform updates infrastructure
docs.text:
• Goal → keep the actual state of infra the same as the desired state in code
  • Desired state → your .tf files | Recorded state → terraform.tfstate | Real state → what actually exists in AWS
  • Every plan / apply:
    1. Read the code (desired)
    2. Read the state file (what Terraform thinks it manages)
    3. Refresh → ask AWS for the current real values
    4. Diff → only resources that differ are created, updated or destroyed
  • Running apply again with no code change → No changes, so Terraform is idempotent

docs.title: The state file
docs.text:
• terraform.tfstate → JSON, written after every apply
  • Maps each resource in code to a real object → aws_vpc.my_vpc ↔ vpc-0abc...
  • Stores → every attribute (IDs, ARNs, tags, IPs), dependencies, provider info, and outputs
  • serial → increases on every write | lineage → unique ID of this state's history, stops one state being written over another
  • terraform.tfstate.backup → the previous version, kept by the local backend only
{
  "version": 4,
  "terraform_version": "1.17.0",
  "serial": 1,
  "lineage": "140fd82e-...",
  "resources": [
    {
      "type": "aws_vpc",
      "name": "my_vpc",
      "instances": [
        { "attributes": { "id": "vpc-0abc...", "cidr_block": "10.0.0.0/16" } }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Why Terraform needs state
docs.text:
• Code says what should exist, AWS has what does exist → state is the link between the two
  • Without it, Terraform can't tell whether aws_vpc.my_vpc already exists or which of 40 VPCs it owns
  • Resource removed from code but still in state → Terraform destroys it
  • Resource created by hand → not in state, Terraform ignores it until terraform import
  • State lost → Terraform forgets it owns anything, next apply tries to create everything again (duplicates or AlreadyExists errors)
  • Drift → someone changes infra in the console; plan shows the difference and apply puts it back to the code

docs.title: Problems with local state
docs.text:
• Lives on one laptop → laptop dies or folder is deleted, state is gone
  • Team → everyone has a different copy, they overwrite each other
  • CI → GitHub Actions can't read your laptop
  • Secrets → DB passwords, keys and tokens are stored in plain text, even with sensitive = true; committing it to Git leaks them
  • No locking → two apply runs at once can corrupt it

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Never edit the state file by hand → use the terraform state commands
  2. Store it remotely → S3, Terraform Cloud, GCS, Azure Blob
  3. Enable locking → no concurrent writes
  4. Enable versioning on the bucket → roll back to an older state if it gets corrupted
  5. Separate state per environment → dev/terraform.tfstate, prod/terraform.tfstate, so a dev mistake can't touch prod
  6. Restrict access → state contains secrets, only Terraform's role and admins should read it
  7. Encrypt at rest and in transit → encrypt = true, HTTPS
  8. Never commit it → .gitignore has *.tfstate and *.tfstate.*

docs.title: Remote backend with S3
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }

  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "your-terraform-state-bucket"
    key          = "dev/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
  • backend "s3" → goes inside the terraform {} block
  • bucket → must already exist before terraform init
  • key → path of the state object inside the bucket; one bucket can hold many states (dev/, prod/, network/)
  • region → region of the state bucket, not where resources are deployed; that's the provider block, and the two can differ
  • encrypt = true → server-side encryption of the state object
  • use_lockfile = true → S3 native locking
  • No variables allowed in the backend block → it's read before variables exist; bucket = var.x fails
  • Any change to the backend block → rerun terraform init

docs.title: The state bucket
docs.text:
Create it outside this config, by hand or in a separate bootstrap config.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket --region us-east-1
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# verify
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket   # "Status": "Enabled"
aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket your-terraform-state-bucket   # "SSEAlgorithm": "AES256"
  • Any region other than us-east-1 → add --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=ap-south-1
  • Don't store state in a bucket the same config creates → chicken-and-egg on init, and destroy would delete the bucket holding its own state
  • Versioning → every apply keeps the old state as a previous version, the backend equivalent of .backup, but keeps all of them
  • Encryption → S3 already encrypts with AES256 by default; setting it makes it explicit
  • Two buckets, two jobs → the backend bucket only stores state and is never in the config | a resource "aws_s3_bucket" is infra the config creates and destroys

docs.title: The state bucket as code (bootstrap)
docs.text:
The same bucket written in Terraform, in its own folder (e.g. state-bootstrap/) whose own state stays local.

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "tf_state" {
  bucket = "your-terraform-state-bucket"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "tf_state" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tf_state.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "tf_state" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tf_state.id

  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm = "AES256"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "tf_state" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.tf_state.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
  • One bucket + three settings → since AWS provider v4 every bucket setting is its own resource pointing at the bucket
  • prevent_destroy = true → any plan that would delete the bucket errors out instead
  • bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tf_state.id → type.name.attribute; for S3 the id is the bucket name, and the reference makes the settings wait for the bucket
  • Same local name tf_state on all four → allowed because the types differ, so the addresses are unique; it's a convention showing they belong together
  • "aws:kms" instead of "AES256" → uses a KMS key (aws/s3 if none is given), adds key access control and audit logs; add bucket_key_enabled = true to cut KMS calls
  • An existing bucket (e.g. made by a script) can't be written like this directly → apply fails with "already exists"; it has to be imported (see Import below) or created under a new name
  • plan → 4 to add

docs.title: S3 native state locking
docs.text:
• Before → locking needed a separate DynamoDB table (dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"): extra service, extra IAM permissions, extra cost
  • Terraform 1.10+ → use_lockfile = true, locking with S3 alone (stable from 1.11); DynamoDB locking is deprecated
  • How it works → S3 conditional writes with the If-None-Match header
    1. Terraform tries to create <key>.tflock, e.g. dev/terraform.tfstate.tflock, only if it doesn't already exist
    2. Doesn't exist → the write succeeds, the lock is acquired
    3. Already exists → S3 rejects it with 412 PreconditionFailed, Terraform reports Error acquiring the state lock
    4. Run finishes → the lock file is deleted (shows as a delete marker when versioning is on)
  • Locks are taken by every command that writes or reads state for a run → plan, apply, destroy, refresh
  • The second run fails immediately by default → -lock-timeout=5m makes it retry and wait
  • Versioning → the course says it's required for native locking; Terraform's docs only strongly recommend it. Enable it anyway, for rollback

docs.title: Migrating local state to S3
docs.text:
1. Create the state bucket with versioning
  2. Add the backend "s3" block
  3. terraform init -migrate-state → answer yes to copy the local state to S3
  4. terraform state pull | head → prints the state from S3
  5. terraform plan → must say No changes

  6. Delete the leftover local terraform.tfstate and terraform.tfstate.backup → they are stale, not used anymore, and still contain account IDs and secrets

  7. .terraform/terraform.tfstate → not infra state; it records which backend this folder uses

  8. Proof the local files were stale → the old backup still had a VPC ID that had since been destroyed and recreated

docs.title: Lab: testing the lock
docs.text:
1. Terminal 1 → terraform destroy, stop at the Enter a value: prompt (the lock is held while waiting)
  2. Terminal 2 → terraform destroy
  3. Terminal 2 fails →
Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Error message: operation error S3: PutObject, https response error StatusCode: 412
api error PreconditionFailed: At least one of the pre-conditions you specified did not hold
Lock Info:
  ID:        <lock-id>
  Path:      <state-bucket>/dev/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       <user>@<hostname>
  Version:   1.17.0
  1. While terminal 1 waits → the S3 console shows dev/terraform.tfstate.tflock next to the state

  2. Answer yes or no in terminal 1 → lock released, .tflock deleted, terminal 2 can run

  3. Operation: OperationTypeApply → destroy is an apply that removes everything

  4. Who → in a team, tells you who is holding the lock
Symptom Cause Fix Error acquiring the state lock Another run holds the lock Wait, or -lock-timeout=5m Lock stays after a crash Process killed mid-run, .tflock left behind terraform force-unlock <lock-id>, only when no run is live Backend configuration changed Backend block edited terraform init -migrate-state or -reconfigure NoSuchBucket on init State bucket doesn't exist Create it first AccessDenied on init IAM user can't read/write the bucket Grant s3:ListBucket, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject on the bucket and key Unsupported argument "use_lockfile" Terraform older than 1.10 Upgrade Terraform
  • Never -lock=false → that's exactly how state gets corrupted
  • Never force-unlock a lock held by a live run

docs.title: Locking vs code conflicts
docs.text:
• Locking stops two runs writing state at the same time → it doesn't merge people's code
  • Person A adds VPC 4 and 5 and applies | Person B never pulled A's code and applies → B's plan destroys VPC 4 and 5, because they're in state but not in B's code
  • A saved plan made before someone else's apply → Error: Saved plan is stale, must re-plan
  • Real fix → Git as the single source of truth, PRs with plan in CI, apply only from main via CI

docs.title: After destroy
docs.text:
• terraform destroy deletes the resources, not the state file → the state stays in S3 with "resources": []
  • serial goes up (destroy is a write), lineage stays the same → the next apply continues the same history
  • terraform state list → prints nothing
  • With versioning on → every old copy and the .tflock delete markers stay visible under Show versions
  • Delete the state object only when the config is retired for good → aws s3 rm s3://<bucket>/dev/terraform.tfstate

docs.title: State commands
docs.text:
None of these touch AWS; they only read or edit the state file. Only apply and destroy change real infra.

  • terraform state list → every address Terraform manages, one per line
aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket
aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.first_bucket
aws_s3_bucket_versioning.first_bucket
aws_vpc.my_vpc
  • terraform state show aws_vpc.my_vpc → every stored attribute of one resource (id, arn, cidr_block, tags, owner_id); takes the full address from state list
  • terraform state pull → downloads the state and prints the JSON; the only way to see the remote file from the terminal | terraform state pull | grep serial
  • terraform state mv <old> <new> → rename a resource in state
  • terraform state rm <address> → Terraform forgets the resource, it keeps running in AWS
  • terraform state push → overwrite remote state with a local file; disaster recovery only
  • terraform show → readable view of the whole current state
  • terraform plan -refresh-only → show drift without changing anything
Command Changes state Changes AWS state list / show / pull No No state mv Renames an entry No state rm Removes an entry No import Adds an entry No destroy Removes entries Deletes resources
  • terraform show vs terraform state show → show takes a file (state or saved plan), state show takes an address
Symptom Cause Fix Failed to read the given file as a state or plan file Ran terraform show aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket, so the address was read as a file name terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket

docs.title: state mv: rename without recreating
docs.text:
1. Rename the block in code → resource "aws_vpc" "my_vpc" becomes resource "aws_vpc" "main", and update every reference to aws_vpc.main.id
  2. terraform plan → shows destroy my_vpc + create main, because Terraform sees a removed resource and a new one
  3. terraform state mv aws_vpc.my_vpc aws_vpc.main

  4. terraform plan → No changes, the same VPC is now tracked under the new address

  5. Use it whenever a resource is renamed or moved into a module, so refactoring never destroys real infra

docs.title: state rm vs destroy
docs.text:
Real resource in AWS In state terraform destroy Deleted Removed terraform state rm Still running Removed
  • After state rm → also delete the block from code, otherwise the next plan wants to create it again and you get a duplicate
  • Use it to keep a resource while destroying the rest, or to hand it over to another config

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
• Import → adopt a resource that already exists in AWS into Terraform's state
  • Needed for anything created outside Terraform → console, CLI, scripts, or a resource dropped with state rm
  • terraform import <address> <real-id> → address = where it lives in your code, id = which real object it is
  • ID format is on each resource's registry page under Import → VPC = vpc-..., S3 bucket and its settings = the bucket name
  • Import only writes state, never code → the resource block must exist first, or it fails with resource address ... does not exist in the configuration
  • Code must describe the real resource → change the code to match AWS, never the other way round, until plan is clean
  • state rm and import are an on/off switch → whatever is in state when destroy runs gets destroyed, imported or not

docs.title: Lab: recovering from state rm
docs.text:
1. terraform state rm aws_vpc.my_vpc → VPC still running, Terraform forgot it
  2. Don't apply → it would create a second VPC
  3. Find the real ID →
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=tf-day3-vpc \
  --query 'Vpcs[].VpcId' --output text
  1. terraform import aws_vpc.my_vpc vpc-xxxxxxxx → Import successful!

  2. terraform state list → all resources back | terraform plan → No changes

  3. It felt like one command because the resource block was still in code; only the state entry was missing

docs.title: Lab: importing a console-made VPC
docs.text:
1. Create a VPC in the console (VPC only)
  2. Read its real settings →
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --vpc-ids vpc-xxxxxxxx \
  --query 'Vpcs[0].{CIDR:CidrBlock,Tags:Tags}'
  1. Write a matching block →
resource "aws_vpc" "demo_import_vpc" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/24"

  tags = {
    Name = "import-vpc"
  }
}
  1. terraform import aws_vpc.demo_import_vpc vpc-xxxxxxxx
  2. terraform plan →
    • No changes → code matches, done
    • ~ update in-place → small difference (tags), fix the code and re-plan
    • -/+ must be replaced → wrong cidr_block, don't apply or the console VPC is deleted
  3. From now on Terraform owns it → terraform destroy deletes it too | to keep it, terraform state rm it and delete the block
  4. Removing the block from code later without state rm → the next plan destroys it

docs.title: Import block and generated code
docs.text:
Terraform 1.5+ can import from code and write the resource block for you.

import {
  to = aws_vpc.demo_import_vpc
  id = "vpc-xxxxxxxx"
}

terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
terraform apply                       # 1 imported, 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed
  • generated.tf → a full resource block filled in from AWS; delete null lines and anything not needed
  • Shows in plan as 1 to import → reviewable in a PR, unlike the CLI command
  • Delete the import {} block after the apply, its job is done
  • Standard way to bring console-built infra into Terraform without writing every block by hand

Quick revision

  • State = map from code to real resources, holds secrets, never commit it
  • Backend → S3 bucket created outside the config, versioning on, encrypt = true, use_lockfile = true
  • Native lock → .tflock + If-None-Match, conflict = 412 PreconditionFailed
  • Locking protects state, Git and CI protect code
  • state rm = forget, import = adopt, state mv = rename, none of them touch AWS
  • Import needs a matching resource block first, then plan must say No changes

Interview points

  • What is the Terraform state file? → JSON mapping resources in code to real infrastructure, used to calculate diffs; may contain secrets
  • Why use a remote backend? → shared state for teams and CI, locking, encryption, versioned backups, no secrets in Git
  • How does S3 native state locking work? → Terraform creates a .tflock object with a conditional write (If-None-Match); if it already exists S3 returns 412 and the second run fails
  • Do you still need DynamoDB for locking? → no, from Terraform 1.10 use_lockfile = true locks with S3 alone; DynamoDB locking is deprecated
  • What happens if the state file is lost? → Terraform no longer knows what it manages; recover from a bucket version, or terraform import the resources back
  • How do you handle a stuck lock? → confirm no run is active, then terraform force-unlock <lock-id>
  • Can you use variables in the backend block? → no, the backend is configured before variables are evaluated; use -backend-config for dynamic values
  • How do you separate environments? → different state keys (dev/, prod/) or separate backends, so a change in one can't affect the other
  • state rm vs destroy? → state rm forgets the resource but leaves it running; destroy deletes the real resource
  • Two engineers apply different code against the same state, what happens? → locking serializes the runs but doesn't merge code; the second plan destroys whatever its code lacks, so use PRs and CI-only applies
  • What does terraform import do? → adds an existing real resource to state under an address in your code; it writes state only, so the matching resource block must exist first
  • How do you bring console-created infra into Terraform? → write matching resource blocks (or use an import block with plan -generate-config-out), import, then adjust code until plan shows no changes
  • You renamed a resource in code and the plan wants to recreate it, what do you do? → terraform state mv <old> <new> so the existing object is tracked under the new address
  • You ran state rm by mistake, how do you recover? → don't apply; find the real ID and terraform import it back, then confirm plan shows no changes
  • Does destroy delete the state file? → no, it deletes the resources and leaves an empty state with a higher serial

docs.title: Type Constraints
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Terraform course day 7

docs.title: Why types
docs.text:
• type on a variable → Terraform checks the value before plan touches anything → wrong input fails early with a clear error
  • No type → defaults to any → anything is accepted, mistakes surface later as confusing provider or API errors
  • Always set type and description on every variable

docs.title: Type family
docs.text:
• Primitive → string, number, bool → a single value
  • Collection → list, set, map → many values, all of the same type
  • Structural → tuple, object → a fixed shape, a different type per element
  • Tuple is to list what object is to map → same structure, but mixed types allowed
Type Access by Duplicates Mixed types Example list(string) position [0] allowed no ["a", "b", "a"] set(string) nothing (loop or contains) dropped no ["a", "b"] map(string) key ["dev"] keys unique no { dev = "t2.micro" } tuple([string, number]) position [0] allowed yes, per position ["t2.micro", 2] object({ a = string }) name .a fields unique yes, per field { a = "x" }

docs.title: Primitive types
docs.text:
• string → text → "t3.micro"
  • number → integers and floats → 2, 3.5
  • bool → true / false
  • Auto conversion → "5" given to a number becomes 5; "true" given to a bool becomes true; "abc" to number errors
variable "instance_type" {
  description = "Type of ec2 instance"
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
}

variable "count_instance" {
  description = "Number of aws instances"
  type        = number
  default     = 1
}

variable "monitoring" {
  description = "enable monitoring"
  type        = bool
  default     = true
}

docs.title: List
docs.text:
• Ordered, allows duplicates, all elements the same type → list(string)
  • Access by index → var.cidr_block[0]
  • length(var.x) → number of elements
  • Pairs with count → resources keyed by index → aws_instance.x[0], [1]
variable "cidr_block" {
  description = "cidr ranges for security group rules"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16", "172.16.0.0/12"]
}

# var.cidr_block[1] → "192.168.0.0/16"

docs.title: Set
docs.text:
• Unordered, unique, all elements the same type → set(string)
  • Duplicates dropped at the moment the variable is read → never created, not deleted later
  • No index → var.regions_allowed[0] → Error: Invalid index
  • Displayed sorted (strings lexically), so the written order is not kept
  • Native uses → for_each (each resource keyed by value) and contains(set, value) (membership check)
  • For sets in for_each → each.key == each.value
  • tolist(set)[0] → works, but that is a list operation; [0] is whatever sorts first
variable "regions_allowed" {
  description = "the regions where it will be created"
  type        = set(string)
  default     = ["us-east-2", "us-east-1", "us-east-1"]
}

# var.regions_allowed → ["us-east-1", "us-east-2"]   (deduped + sorted)

docs.title: List vs set: why it matters
docs.text:
• count + list → identity is position → remove a middle item → every later index shifts → those resources replaced
  • for_each + set → identity is value → remove an item → only that resource destroyed
List: apple banana orange apple  → remove banana
  [0] apple  → apple    no change
  [1] banana → orange   replaced
  [2] orange → apple    replaced
  [3] apple  → (gone)   destroyed

Set: { apple, banana, orange }  → remove banana
  ["apple"]  no change
  ["banana"] destroyed
  ["orange"] no change
  • Why providers use sets → e.g. vpc_security_group_ids is a set → reordering IDs shows no diff in plan
  • Pick a set when swapping two items wouldn't change the meaning → regions to deploy to, bucket names, SG IDs, users
  • Pick a list when order or position matters → AZs mapped to CIDRs by index, priority order, "take the first one"

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
• Key = value pairs; keys are always strings and unique; values all the same type → map(string)
  • Access by key → var.instance_types["dev"] | var.instance_types[var.environment]
  • No index → var.m[0] errors
  • lookup(map, key, default) → safe access when the key may be missing
  • keys(map) / values(map) → lists, sorted by key
  • merge(a, b) → combines maps; on a key clash b wins
  • tags = { ... } is just a map
  • Pairs with for_each → each.key = key, each.value = value (unlike sets, they differ)
variable "tag-ec2" {
  description = "ec2-instance tags"
  type        = map(string)
  default = {
    Name        = "demo-tag"
    Environment = "dev"
    created_by  = "terraform-aditya"
  }
}

variable "instance_types" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    dev     = "t2.micro"
    staging = "t3.small"
    prod    = "t3.large"
  }
}

# instance_type = var.instance_types[var.environment]
  • for_each over a map → key and value both used:
variable "buckets" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    logs    = "Enabled"
    backups = "Suspended"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "b" {
  for_each = var.buckets
  bucket   = "${local.prefix}-${each.key}"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "v" {
  for_each = var.buckets
  bucket   = aws_s3_bucket.b[each.key].id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = each.value
  }
}

docs.title: Element type is required
docs.text:
• map() / list() / set() with empty brackets → syntax error
  • map(any) → Terraform infers one type for all values → { a = "x", b = 5 } becomes map(string) → 5 silently turns into "5"
  • Bare map → legacy shorthand for map(any) → still works, avoid
  • Spell out the element type → map(string), list(number); for different types per key → use object

docs.title: Tuple
docs.text:
• Fixed length, ordered, each position has its own type → tuple([number, string, number])
  • Wrong length or wrong type order → error
  • Access by index like a list → var.ingress_value[0]
  • Weak point → [443, "tcp", 443] doesn't say what each value means
  • Rarely declared in real code; prefer object
  • Any [...] literal is a tuple until converted to the declared type → why error messages mention "tuple" for a list variable
variable "ingress_value" {
  type    = tuple([number, string, number])
  default = [443, "tcp", 443]
}

# from_port   = var.ingress_value[0]   → 443
# ip_protocol = var.ingress_value[1]   → "tcp"
# to_port     = var.ingress_value[2]   → 443

docs.title: Object
docs.text:
• Named fields, each with its own type → object({ instance_type = string, count = number })
  • Access by name → var.server.instance_type
  • Every declared field must be given; wrong field type → error; extra undeclared fields → silently dropped
  • Field order doesn't matter (unlike tuple)
  • optional(type, default) → field can be omitted (Terraform 1.3+) → count = optional(number, 1)
variable "server" {
  description = "ec2 instance settings"
  type = object({
    instance_type = string
    count         = optional(number, 1)
    monitoring    = optional(bool, false)
  })
  default = {
    instance_type = "t3.micro"
    monitoring    = true
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  count         = var.server.count
  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = var.server.instance_type
  monitoring    = var.server.monitoring
}
  • The same ingress rule as an object → readable, self-documenting:
variable "ingress" {
  type = object({
    from_port = number
    protocol  = string
    to_port   = number
  })
  default = { from_port = 443, protocol = "tcp", to_port = 443 }
}

# from_port = var.ingress.from_port

docs.title: Tuple vs object
docs.text: Tuple Object Identified by position [0] name .instance_type Syntax [ ] { } Order matters yes no Optional fields no yes, optional() Readability poor, what does 2 mean clear, count = 2

docs.title: Map vs object
docs.text:
• Map → any keys decided by the caller, one value type → a collection of things
  • Object → fixed field names decided in the type, mixed types → one thing with properties
  • Combined → map(object({...})) → many things, each with the same shape → the most common for_each pattern
variable "servers" {
  type = map(object({
    instance_type = string
    monitoring    = bool
  }))
  default = {
    web = { instance_type = "t2.micro", monitoring = false }
    api = { instance_type = "t3.small", monitoring = true }
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "s" {
  for_each      = var.servers
  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = each.value.instance_type
  monitoring    = each.value.monitoring
  tags          = { Name = each.key }
}
  • list(object({...})) → same idea but ordered and index-keyed → fine for count, worse for for_each

docs.title: Validation blocks
docs.text:
• Type checks the shape; validation checks business rules → allowed values, formats, ranges
  • condition must be true, else error_message is shown at plan
  • Several validation blocks per variable are allowed
  • Since Terraform 1.9 a condition can reference other variables
variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  default = "dev"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "preprod", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "Environment must be dev, staging, preprod or prod."
  }
}

variable "vpc_cidr" {
  type    = string
  default = "10.0.0.0/16"

  validation {
    condition     = can(cidrhost(var.vpc_cidr, 0))
    error_message = "VPC CIDR must be a valid IPv4 CIDR block."
  }
}

variable "count_instance" {
  type    = number
  default = 1

  validation {
    condition     = var.count_instance >= 1 && var.count_instance <= 3
    error_message = "Instance count must be between 1 and 3."
  }
}

variable "region" {
  type    = string
  default = "us-east-1"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(var.regions_allowed, var.region)
    error_message = "Region must be one of the allowed regions."
  }
}
  • contains(list_or_set, value) → allowed-values check
  • can(expr) → true if expr doesn't error → format checks like cidrhost, regex
  • length(var.x) > 0 → non-empty check
  • can(regex("^t3\\.", var.instance_type)) → pattern check

docs.title: Type conversion functions
docs.text:
• tolist(set) → set → list (sorted order)
  • toset(list) → list → set (dedupes) → common before for_each
  • tomap({...}) → object → map (all values must convert to one type)
  • tonumber("5") → 5 | tostring(5) → "5" | tobool("true") → true
  • Prefer declaring the right type over converting at every use

docs.title: Lab: type constraints on EC2, SG and S3
docs.text:
Config (course day 7, ~> 6.0 AWS provider, S3 backend with use_lockfile):

# variables.tf
variable "cidr_block" {
  description = "cidr ranges for security group rules"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16", "172.16.0.0/12"]
}

variable "regions_allowed" {
  description = "the regions where it will be created"
  type        = set(string)
  default     = ["us-east-1", "us-east-2"]
}

variable "tag-ec2" {
  description = "ec2-instance tags"
  type        = map(string)
  default = {
    Name        = "demo-tag"
    Environment = "dev"
    created_by  = "terraform-aditya"
  }
}

variable "ingress_value" {
  type    = tuple([number, string, number])
  default = [443, "tcp", 443]
}

# main.tf
resource "aws_instance" "my_instance" {
  count                       = var.count_instance
  ami                         = "ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
  instance_type               = var.instance_type
  region                      = tolist(var.regions_allowed)[0]   # resource-level region needs AWS provider v6+
  monitoring                  = var.monitoring
  associate_public_ip_address = var.public_ip
  tags                        = var.tag-ec2
}

# sg.tf
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "allow_tls_ipv4" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.allow_tls.id
  cidr_ipv4         = var.cidr_block[1]
  from_port         = var.ingress_value[0]
  ip_protocol       = var.ingress_value[1]
  to_port           = var.ingress_value[2]
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "allow_all_traffic_ipv4" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.allow_tls.id
  cidr_ipv4         = var.cidr_block[0]
  ip_protocol       = "-1"
}

What each type does here:

  • list(string) → cidr_block[1] / [0] → pick CIDRs by position
  • set(string) → regions_allowed → unique regions; needs tolist() to pick one
  • map(string) → tag-ec2 → passed straight to tags
  • tuple([number, string, number]) → ingress_value → port, protocol, port by position

Set demo in for_each (one instance per region, AMI looked up per region because AMI IDs are regional):

data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  for_each    = var.regions_allowed
  region      = each.key
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["099720109477"]   # Canonical

  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "per_region" {
  for_each      = var.regions_allowed
  region        = each.key
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu[each.key].id
  instance_type = var.instance_type
  tags          = { Name = "${local.prefix}-${each.key}" }
}
  • plan shows aws_instance.per_region["us-east-1"] and ["us-east-2"] → keyed by value
  • A duplicate region in the default → still only 2 instances
  • count and for_each can't be used on the same resource

Check types in the console:

terraform console

> var.cidr_block[0]
"10.0.0.0/8"
> var.regions_allowed[0]
Error: Invalid index
> tolist(var.regions_allowed)[0]
"us-east-1"
> var.tag-ec2["created_by"]
"terraform-aditya"
> var.ingress_value[1]
"tcp"
> toset(["a", "b", "a"])
toset(["a", "b"])
> exit

Errors I hit:

Symptom Cause Fix Error: Invalid index on var.regions_allowed[0] sets have no positions tolist(var.regions_allowed)[0], or use the set natively with for_each InvalidParameterValue: Invalid value 'us-east-1' for InstanceType instance_type was fed a region value; AWS rejects it at apply, validate can't catch it point instance_type at the instance type variable; grep -n instance_type *.tf *.tfvars Apply failed halfway, bucket and SG already created apply is not atomic; created resources are already in state fix the code, run apply again → only the failed resource is created Unsupported argument "region" on a resource resource-level region only exists in AWS provider v6+ version = "~> 6.0" in required_providers, then terraform init -upgrade Invalid type specification for map() element type missing map(string) Resource block not closed } after tags closed only tags add the resource's closing }; terraform fmt + validate catch it InvalidAMIID.NotFound AMI IDs are per region look up the AMI with a data "aws_ami" per region

Check and deploy:

  1. terraform fmt
  2. terraform validate
  3. terraform plan
  4. terraform apply
  5. terraform destroy when done (EC2 costs money)

Quick revision

  • Primitive → string, number, bool | Collection → list, set, map | Structural → tuple, object
  • List → position, dupes | Set → unique, no index | Map → key → value
  • Tuple → fixed types by position | Object → fixed types by name
  • count + list → index shift recreates | for_each + set/map → stable keys
  • optional(type, default) → omit object fields
  • validation → contains, can, length, regex
  • tolist / toset / tomap → convert when needed

Interview points

  • Why declare types on variables? → bad input fails at plan with a clear message instead of a confusing provider error mid-apply
  • List vs set? → list is ordered, allows duplicates and has index access; set is unordered, unique and has no index
  • Why use a set instead of a list? → for_each needs stable keys; reordering causes no diff; duplicates are impossible
  • Why is for_each preferred over count? → count keys by index, so removing a middle item shifts and recreates later resources; for_each keys by value, so only the removed one is destroyed
  • Can you index a set? → no, Invalid index; use tolist() or loop over it with for_each
  • each.key vs each.value? → same for a set; for a map, key is the map key and value is its value
  • Map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed field names with their own types
  • Tuple vs object? → both have a fixed shape with mixed types; tuple by position, object by name; object is more readable and supports optional()
  • What does map(any) do with { a = "x", b = 5 }? → picks one type for all values, so 5 becomes "5"
  • How do you make an object field optional? → optional(type, default), Terraform 1.3+
  • How do you restrict a variable to allowed values? → validation block with contains([...], var.x) and an error_message
  • What's the most common real-world for_each type? → map(object({...})): many items, each with the same shape
  • Does terraform validate catch a wrong value like a region in instance_type? → no, it checks syntax and types only; the AWS API rejects it at apply

docs.title: Variables, Locals & Outputs
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Terraform course day 5

docs.title: Two ways to classify variables
docs.text:
• Based on purpose → input (variable), local (locals), output (output)
  • Based on value → type constraints: primitive, complex, any

docs.title: Based on purpose
docs.text:
Block Set from outside Used as Like Input variable Yes var.x function parameter Local locals No local.x variable inside a function Output output No, read from outside terraform output x return value
  • Input → a value coming into the code; same code, different values per run or environment
  • Local → a value the code computes itself, once, and reuses
  • Output → a value going out after apply, for humans, scripts and other configs

docs.title: Input variables
docs.text:
variable "environment" {
  type        = string
  default     = "dev"
  description = "Environment name, used in names and tags"
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}
  • type → what kind of value is allowed; a wrong type fails before anything touches AWS
  • default → the fallback, used only when nothing else gives a value; makes the variable optional
  • No default → required, Terraform asks for it in the terminal (Enter a value:)
  • description → shown in prompts and docs, always write one
  • sensitive = true → hidden in plan output, still stored in plain text in state
  • validation { } → custom rules, e.g. only allow dev, stage, prod
  • default must be a fixed value → no var.x, no resource attributes, no functions
  • The code never changes between environments → default = "dev" stays in the file, the value is decided when Terraform runs

docs.title: Type constraints
docs.text:
Primitive → a single value

variable "name"    { type = string }   # "web"
variable "port"    { type = number }   # 8080
variable "enabled" { type = bool }     # true

Complex → a collection

variable "azs"    { type = list(string) }                         # ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
variable "users"  { type = set(string) }                          # ["alice", "bob"]
variable "tags"   { type = map(string) }                          # { env = "dev", team = "ops" }
variable "server" { type = object({ name = string, port = number }) }
variable "pair"   { type = tuple([string, number]) }              # ["web", 80]
  • list → ordered, duplicates allowed, all items the same type, any length
  • set → unordered, no duplicates
  • map → any keys, every value the same type
  • object → fixed keys, each with its own type
  • tuple → fixed length, a type per position
  • list vs tuple → same type and any length vs fixed length with a type per position
  • map vs object → any keys with one value type vs fixed keys with their own types
  • any → no type check, also what you get without type; convenient but loses safety
  • null → not a type but a value meaning "not set"; an argument set to null is the same as leaving it out, so the provider default applies

docs.title: Locals
docs.text:
• A local is a nickname for a value → write it once, use it everywhere
  • Use it for values that are repeated or built from other values
locals {
  prefix = "${var.environment}-ap14"
}
  • local.prefix → "dev-ap14"
  • Defined in locals (plural), referenced as local. (singular)
  • Can use anything → variables, other locals, resource attributes, functions, conditions
  • Can't be set from outside → -var and tfvars have no effect on it
  • No type argument → the type is inferred from the value
  • Check a local without creating anything →
terraform console
> local.prefix
"dev-ap14"
> exit
terraform console -var="environment=prod"
> local.prefix
"prod-ap14"

docs.title: Variable vs local
docs.text:
variable locals Who sets the value Whoever runs Terraform Only the code Changes per run without editing code Yes No Expressions and references No, default is a fixed value Yes Type check type = ... Inferred Used as var.x local.x
  • The value should differ between runs or environments (region, env, instance size) → variable
  • The value is derived from other values or repeated in many places (name prefix, common tags) → local
  • Restaurant version → variable = the order form the customer fills in, local = the kitchen's own recipe

docs.title: Locals in real projects
docs.text:
• Common tags → every resource gets identical Project, Environment, Owner, ManagedBy tags for cost reports and ownership
  • Naming convention → one name_prefix like ${var.project}-${var.env}, nobody types names by hand
  • Environment-based values → instance_type = var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.small" : "t3.micro"
  • Calculations once → subnet_cidrs = [for i in range(3) : cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 8, i)]
  • Shortening long expressions → account_id = data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id
  • Don't overdo it → a local used once, or locals chained five deep, make code harder to read

docs.title: Repeated tags: the problem locals solve
docs.text:
Without a local → the same tags typed on every resource; adding Owner means editing every block and missing one.

locals {
  tags = {
    Environment = var.environment
    ManagedBy   = "terraform"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "first_bucket" {
  bucket = local.bucket
  tags   = local.tags
}
  • One change in locals → every resource using local.tags follows
  • tags = local.tags alone → the resource gets only the shared tags and loses its own Name

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
• merge(map1, map2, ...) → joins maps into one map
  • tags takes one map, and a resource needs the shared tags plus its own Name → tags can't be written twice, so the maps are merged
tags = merge(local.tags, {
  Name  = "${local.prefix}-demo-bucket"
  Vpcid = aws_vpc.my_vpc.id
})
  • Read it as "the shared tags, plus these for this resource"
  • Same key in both maps → the later map wins → merge({ env = "dev" }, { env = "prod" }) gives { env = "prod" }
  • Try it → terraform console, then merge({a = 1}, {b = 2})
  • Dropping Vpcid = aws_vpc.my_vpc.id from the tags also drops the implicit dependency on the VPC

docs.title: Conditional expression
docs.text:
• condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false
  • var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.small" : "t3.micro" → prod gets t3.small, everything else t3.micro

docs.title: Ways to set a variable (precedence)
docs.text:
Lowest to highest priority; a later source overrides an earlier one.

  1. default in the variable block
  2. Environment variable → export TF_VAR_environment=stage
  3. terraform.tfvars → loaded automatically
  4. terraform.tfvars.json → loaded automatically, after terraform.tfvars
  5. *.auto.tfvars / *.auto.tfvars.json → loaded automatically, in alphabetical order

  6. -var="environment=prod" and -var-file="prod.tfvars" on the command line → the last one given wins

  7. No value from anywhere and no default → Terraform prompts for it

  8. Memory trick → the closer the value is to the moment you run the command, the stronger it is
  9. prod.tfvars / dev.tfvars → not loaded automatically, only with -var-file; this is how teams keep one file per environment
# terraform.tfvars  (plain name = value lines, no variable block)
environment = "demo"
bucket_name = "terraform-demo-bucket"

docs.title: TF_VAR_ environment variables
docs.text:
export TF_VAR_environment=stage
echo $TF_VAR_environment
terraform console          # > var.environment → "stage"
unset TF_VAR_environment
terraform console          # > var.environment → "dev"
  • Terraform reads any shell variable named TF_VAR_<name> as the value of variable "<name>"; the name is case-sensitive
  • export → makes it visible to programs run from this terminal; it lasts until the terminal closes or unset
  • Don't put it in ~/.bashrc → you forget it's set and deploy the wrong environment
  • Used for → CI jobs setting values per environment, and secrets like TF_VAR_db_password kept out of files and Git
  • Weaker than tfvars files → with terraform.tfvars setting environment = "demo", TF_VAR_environment has no effect

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
output "bucket_name" {
  description = "Name of the S3 bucket"
  value       = aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket.bucket
}

output "environment" {
  value = var.environment
}

output "tags" {
  value = local.tags
}
  • Printed at the end of every apply, stored in state
  • Can show a resource attribute, an input, or a local → handy to check what a local computed
  • terraform output → all outputs, any time after apply
  • terraform output bucket_name → one output
  • terraform output -raw bucket_name → bare value without quotes, for scripts → aws s3 ls s3://$(terraform output -raw bucket_name)
  • terraform output -json → everything as JSON, for scripts and CI
  • sensitive = true → shown as (sensitive value) in the CLI, still in state
  • Other configs and modules read outputs → that's how one stack passes a VPC ID to another

docs.title: Unique names with random_string
docs.text:
resource "random_string" "suffix" {
  length  = 6
  special = false
  upper   = false
}

locals {
  full_bucket_name = "${var.environment}-${var.bucket_name}-${random_string.suffix.result}"
}
  • From the random provider (hashicorp/random) → creates nothing in AWS, only generates values; add it to required_providers and run terraform init
  • special = false, upper = false → S3 names allow only lowercase letters, numbers and -
  • Generated once and stored in state → it doesn't change on every run
  • Solves globally unique bucket names without hand-made suffixes

docs.title: File layout
docs.text:
provider.tf       → terraform {} and provider {}
variables.tf      → input variables
locals.tf         → locals
main.tf           → resources
output.tf         → outputs
terraform.tfvars  → values for the variables
  • Terraform loads every .tf file in the folder as one config → the split is only for humans, like block order
  • Standard layout in real repos

docs.title: Lab: refactoring the day 4 config
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }

  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "your-terraform-state-bucket"
    key          = "dev/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

variable "aws_region" {
  type        = string
  default     = "us-east-1"
  description = "AWS region to deploy into"
}

variable "environment" {
  type        = string
  default     = "dev"
  description = "Environment name, used in names and tags"
}

locals {
  prefix   = "${var.environment}-ap14"
  bucket   = "${var.environment}-bucket-${var.aws_region}-ap14"
  name_vpc = "${var.environment}-second-vpc"

  tags = {
    Environment = var.environment
    ManagedBy   = "terraform"
  }
}

resource "aws_vpc" "my_vpc" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"

  tags = merge(local.tags, {
    Name = "${local.prefix}-my-vpc"
  })
}

resource "aws_vpc" "second_vpc" {
  cidr_block = "10.1.0.0/16"

  tags = merge(local.tags, {
    Name = local.name_vpc
  })
}

resource "aws_instance" "my_instance" {
  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  tags = merge(local.tags, {
    Name = "${local.prefix}-my-demo"
  })
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "first_bucket" {
  bucket = local.bucket

  tags = merge(local.tags, {
    Name  = local.bucket
    Vpcid = aws_vpc.my_vpc.id
  })
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "first_bucket" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "first_bucket" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.first_bucket.id

  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm = "aws:kms"
    }
    bucket_key_enabled = true
  }
}
  1. terraform fmt and terraform validate
  2. terraform plan → names like dev-ap14-my-vpc, dev-bucket-us-east-1-ap14
  3. terraform plan -var="environment=prod" → every name and tag switches to prod, no code edited
  4. terraform destroy when done → the EC2 instance costs money while running
Symptom Cause Fix Blocks of type "provider" are not expected here provider block placed inside terraform {} Move it to the top level Variable declared but changes nothing aws_region not used in the provider region = var.aws_region Bucket named for one region, created in another Name uses var.aws_region, provider is hardcoded Use the variable in both Environment = dev on a prod resource Tag hardcoded instead of var.environment Take every tag from local.tags dev-bucketus-east-1-ap14 Missing - in the interpolation Check with terraform console → local.bucket Plan shows -/+ on the bucket Bucket name changed, S3 can't rename Expected for a lab bucket; fails with BucketNotEmpty if it has objects Plan wants to destroy a VPC you didn't touch Its block was removed but it's still in state (e.g. an imported one) Put the block back, or terraform state rm it EC2 instance not in your VPC No subnet_id, so it lands in the default VPC Add a subnet in your VPC and set subnet_id AMI not found after changing region AMI IDs are region-specific Look it up with a data "aws_ami" source VpcLimitExceeded Default limit of 5 VPCs per region, default VPC included Destroy unused VPCs Empty locals {} Valid but useless Remove it or put repeated values in it
  • Two VPCs with the same CIDR → AWS allows it, but overlapping VPCs can never be peered; give each its own range
  • Switching environment with one fixed backend key → not a separate environment; it renames the dev resources and replaces the bucket in the same state. Separate environments need separate state (different key, or workspaces)

Quick revision

  • Input = var.x from outside, local = local.x computed inside, output = printed after apply
  • Precedence → default < TF_VAR_ < terraform.tfvars < .tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var / -var-file
  • merge(local.tags, { Name = ... }) → shared tags plus the resource's own
  • terraform console → test any variable, local or function without touching AWS
  • One state per environment, not one variable per environment

Interview points

  • Variable vs local? → a variable is an input set from outside per run; a local is a value computed inside the module and can't be overridden
  • Why can't a variable's default use another variable? → defaults must be fixed values; computed values belong in locals
  • What is the variable precedence order? → default, then TF_VAR_ env vars, terraform.tfvars, terraform.tfvars.json, *.auto.tfvars in alphabetical order, and -var / -var-file on the command line last and strongest
  • terraform.tfvars vs prod.tfvars? → terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars load automatically; any other name loads only with -var-file
  • How do you pass secrets to Terraform? → TF_VAR_ env vars or a secrets manager, mark the variable sensitive = true; the value still lands in state, so the state must be protected
  • How do you enforce common tags on all resources? → a common_tags local merged into each resource's tags with merge(), or the AWS provider's default_tags block
  • list vs set vs tuple? → list is ordered with duplicates, set is unordered and unique, tuple has a fixed length with a type per position
  • map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed keys with their own types
  • What are outputs used for? → showing values after apply, feeding scripts via -raw / -json, and passing values between modules and stacks
  • Does sensitive = true hide a value from state? → no, only from CLI output
  • How do you get unique S3 bucket names? → add a suffix from random_string (stored in state so it stays stable) or include account and region in the name
  • Is changing a variable enough to create a separate prod environment? → no, with the same backend key it modifies the same resources; prod needs its own state
